items.title: The Confrontation
items.question: Camus locates the absurd neither in the world alone nor in humans alone, but in their confrontation: our appetite for meaning meeting a silent world.
items.correctExplanation: True. The absurd is born of the encounter — longing plus silence. Remove either term and it vanishes; divorce, not desert, is the diagnosis.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Neither a mute universe without questioners nor satisfied minds without questions produces the absurd. Camus places it precisely at the collision: the divorce between appetite and answer.
items.lessonContent:
Absurdity lives in encounters, not in objects.
Longing plus silence equals the full formula.
Single-term explanations miss the confrontation.
Diagnose divorces, not deserts.
Share this: name one appetite the world leaves unanswered.

items.title: The Despair Charge
items.question: Because Camus starts from meaninglessness, his philosophy ultimately endorses despair and resignation as the honest response.
items.correctExplanation: False. The absurd diagnoses; revolt prescribes. Despair surrenders the confrontation Camus demands we maintain — lucidity without resignation is the whole ethic.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Starting from silence, Camus builds revolt, freedom, and passion — never resignation. Despair agrees with the silence; revolt answers it. The Myth's arc climbs from diagnosis to defiance.
items.lessonContent:
Diagnoses are not prescriptions — check the arc.
Revolt answers what despair merely echoes.
Lucidity without resignation is the demanded stance.
Follow arguments past their first chapter.
Share this: answer one silence with action today.

items.title: The Happy Condemned
items.question: Camus concludes that Sisyphus — condemned to roll his rock eternally — must be imagined happy, his lucid revolt filling the struggle with meaning.
items.correctExplanation: True. Conscious fate becomes owned fate: each descent Sisyphus chooses his rock, and the struggle itself suffices. Happiness here is defiance, not comfort.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The famous closing inverts the punishment: lucidity converts sentence into choice, and chosen struggle fills the heart. 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy' crowns revolt, not resignation.
items.lessonContent:
Chosen struggle fills hearts that sentences empty.
Lucidity converts punishments into positions.
Sufficiency lives inside effort, not arrival.
Own the descent and the rock lightens.
Share this: choose one burden consciously today.

items.title: The Only Door
items.question: Camus argues that suicide is the one truly serious philosophical problem because a meaningless life logically compels self-destruction.
items.correctExplanation: False. Suicide is the serious question precisely because Camus answers no: living without appeal refutes it. The problem is real; the compulsion is denied.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Camus opens with suicide as the fundamental question in order to reject it — the absurd must be lived, not fled. Evading the confrontation settles nothing; revolt is the argued answer.
items.lessonContent:
Serious questions need not compel dark answers.
Opening with suicide frames the stakes, not the verdict.
Living-without-appeal is the argued alternative.
Read past the first sentence of every provocation.
Share this: live one question instead of fleeing it.

items.title: The Second Suicide
items.question: Camus rejects not only physical suicide but also 'philosophical suicide' — the leap of faith that escapes the absurd through God or absolutes.
items.correctExplanation: True. Leaps to God, Reason, or eternity dodge the confrontation as surely as death. Camus demands the tension be kept, not dissolved by either exit.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Kierkegaard's leap and Husserl's essences both exit the absurd through transcendence — elegant evasions Camus refuses. Two suicides, one physical, one intellectual; revolt rejects both doors.
items.lessonContent:
Evasions wear sacred and scholarly costumes alike.
Tension kept beats tension dissolved.
Leaps exit; revolt remains.
Suspect every exit that ends the questioning.
Share this: keep one tension unresolved this week.

items.title: The Permanent No
items.question: Camusian revolt means defiance without hope of final victory — a permanent 'no' to one's condition paired with living fully inside it.
items.correctExplanation: True. Revolt refuses consolation and surrender together: no to fate, yes to life. Permanence is the point — a confrontation maintained, never won.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Revolt is not revolution (no final victory promised) but stance: lucid refusal plus passionate living. Temporary rebellion seeks outcomes; revolt is the outcome — maintained tension as a way of life.
items.lessonContent:
Stances outlast campaigns when no victory exists.
Refusal plus passion defines the position.
Maintained tension is itself a way of life.
Seek no exit from the confrontation.
Share this: hold one tension without resolving it.

items.title: The Answered World
items.question: Even if the universe answered every human longing completely, Camus's absurd would stubbornly survive as a basic mood.
items.correctExplanation: False. Answered longing dissolves the confrontation that births the absurd — no silence, no divorce. The absurd is conditional, not atmospheric.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The absurd needs both terms: appetite and silence. A responding world ends the divorce, and with it the concept. Conditionality is the doctrine's honesty — remove the cause, remove the effect.
items.lessonContent:
Conditional doctrines die with their conditions.
Both terms are load-bearing, neither decorative.
Moods pass; structures persist while fed.
Test concepts by removing each pillar.
Share this: imagine one longing fully answered.

items.title: The Quantity Ethic
items.question: Don Juan's endless loves exemplify Camus's ethic of quantity — living the most experiences possible rather than the deepest single one.
items.correctExplanation: True. With no ultimate hierarchy of lives, Don Juan multiplies experience: quantity becomes the absurd ethic. Each love lived fully, none mistaken for eternity.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Don Juan doesn't love deeply once but completely each time — the ethic of quantity over illusory depth. Where eternity is unavailable, multiplicity is honesty.
items.lessonContent:
Multiplicity can be honesty where eternity is closed.
Quantity becomes ethic when hierarchies collapse.
Each fully, none forever: the Don Juan rule.
Depth-illusions waste what breadth could live.
Share this: multiply one experience this month.

items.title: The Many Lives
items.question: Camus's actor lives absurdly well by dying many stage deaths — sampling countless lives within one brief span.
items.correctExplanation: True. The actor compresses centuries into evenings, living and dying on schedule. Brief time, maximum lives: quantity's theatrical form.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Where Don Juan multiplies loves, the actor multiplies selves — Hamlet tonight, Lear tomorrow. One lifespan, countless traversals: the absurd arithmetic of the stage.
items.lessonContent:
Selves can multiply like loves and days.
Stages compress centuries into evenings.
Traversal beats duration in absurd arithmetic.
Sample widely within narrow spans.
Share this: live one borrowed life this weekend.

items.title: The Day's Master
items.question: The conqueror — Camus's man of action — masters his days by choosing fully within limits, demanding everything from the present hour.
items.correctExplanation: True. Conquerors act without appeal to tomorrow: efficiency, adventure, chosen struggle. Mastery of hours replaces mastery of history.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The conqueror knows victories fade and acts anyway — present-tense fullness over future-tense salvation. Days, not destinies, are the conquerable territory.
items.lessonContent:
Hours are conquerable where histories are not.
Present-tense fullness beats future-tense salvation.
Act without appeal to tomorrow's ledger.
Choose fully inside acknowledged limits.
Share this: master one hour completely today.

items.title: The Licensed Blade
items.question: Because revolt rejects all limits, Camus permits revolutionary violence without restraint in the name of freedom.
items.correctExplanation: False. The Rebel draws the line: revolt says no to oppression, including the rebel's own slide into executioner. 'Neither victim nor executioner' bounds every blade.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Camus's rebel refuses murder's logic even for liberation — unlimited violence repeats the tyranny it claims to fight. Limits are revolt's spine, not its betrayal.
items.lessonContent:
Rebellions must refuse their own tyrannies.
Means infect ends; blades cut both ways.
Bounded revolt outlasts absolute license.
Check every liberation for new executioners.
Share this: name one cause that ate its own.

items.title: The Twin Refusal
items.question: 'Neither victim nor executioner' compresses Camus's rebel ethic: refuse suffering oppression and refuse inflicting it.
items.correctExplanation: True. The twin refusal draws revolt's clean line: resist the executioner without becoming one. Symmetry of refusal is the whole morality.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Victimhood accepted breeds complicity; executionerhood seized breeds tyranny. The rebel's narrow path threads between — refusing both chairs at the violent table.
items.lessonContent:
Twin refusals draw cleaner lines than single ones.
Resist without replicating the violence.
Narrow paths thread between two chairs.
Symmetry of refusal is complete morality.
Share this: refuse one of each today.

items.title: The Open License
items.question: Camus's absurd implies that, with no ultimate values, literally everything is permitted and no act can be condemned.
items.correctExplanation: False. Camus explicitly denies the license: revolt founds values — human solidarity, limits, refusal of murder. Absence of absolutes is not absence of ethics.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'Everything is permitted' is the slogan Camus refutes, not preaches: revolt generates its own limits from shared confrontation. Ethics without absolutes still condemns the executioner.
items.lessonContent:
Absence of absolutes never equals absence of ethics.
Shared confrontation founds shared limits.
Refuted slogans get misattributed constantly.
Read what follows the famous premises.
Share this: correct one 'everything permitted' misuse.

items.title: The Owned Hour
items.question: For the absurd man, the present moment is the only secure possession — neither past nor future can be owned, so full presence is the demand.
items.correctExplanation: True. Hope mortgages presence to futures that never pay; nostalgia spends it backward. Only the hour in hand is ownable — live it entirely.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Past is uneditable, future unwritten; presence alone is property. Camus's temporal ethic concentrates all wealth into now — spend it completely or lose it doubly.
items.lessonContent:
Presence alone is ownable property.
Hope mortgages hours to nonpaying futures.
Nostalgia spends wealth backward.
Concentrate riches into the hour in hand.
Share this: own one full hour today.

items.title: The Afterlife Exit
items.question: Hoping for an afterlife that redeems suffering counts, for Camus, as another escape from the absurd rather than an answer to it.
items.correctExplanation: True. Deferred justice dissolves the confrontation by promising reconciliation — philosophical suicide in eschatological dress. Revolt wants no settlement, here or hereafter.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Afterlife hope trades present lucidity for future compensation, exiting the tension Camus demands we keep. Settlement refused is the doctrine's spine — no deals, temporal or eternal.
items.lessonContent:
Deferred settlements exit present tensions.
Compensation promises dissolve confrontations.
No-deals policies span time and eternity.
Keep the tension; refuse the settlement.
Share this: live one hour settlement-free.

items.title: The Hoping Stone
items.question: Sisyphus should hope that this time the rock stays balanced at the summit, since hope would lighten his eternal task.
items.correctExplanation: False. Hope betrays lucidity — it mortgages the present to a future the gods control. Sisyphus owns only the push; hoping outsources his happiness to the summit.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Hope would convert revolt into waiting, surrendering the owned hour to unowned outcomes. The myth's ethic forbids exactly this comfort: no hope, full living.
items.lessonContent:
Hope can betray lucidity it claims to serve.
Mortgaged presents enrich no one.
Owned pushes beat outsourced summits.
Comforts that surrender stance are traps.
Share this: push one rock hopelessly and happily.

items.title: The Cold Proof
items.question: Camus derives the absurd through strict logical deduction from self-evident first principles, like a geometer proving theorems.
items.correctExplanation: False. He begins from a feeling — the encounter with strangeness, nausea at routine — and reasons outward. Absurd reasoning starts in experience, not axioms.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The Myth opens with weariness, disgust, the weight of days: phenomenology first, logic after. Geometers deduce; Camus describes, then follows the description where it leads.
items.lessonContent:
Feelings can found philosophies legitimately.
Description precedes deduction in lived thought.
Axioms miss what encounters reveal.
Start from nausea, not from nothing.
Share this: describe one strange Tuesday fully.

items.title: The World Alone
items.question: A universe empty of all conscious beings would still contain the absurd as a property of silent matter itself.
items.correctExplanation: False. No questioners, no confrontation, no absurd — silent matter alone is merely silent. The concept needs its human term absolutely.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Absurdity is relational: remove minds and only muteness remains, unopposed and unabsurd. Properties of encounters vanish with either party.
items.lessonContent:
Relational properties need both relata present.
Encounters vanish with either party gone.
Muteness alone is not absurdity.
Test attributions by subtraction.
Share this: subtract minds from one landscape.

items.title: The Mind Alone
items.question: Human longing by itself — even in a world that answered every question — would still generate the absurd from within.
items.correctExplanation: False. Satisfied longing is not absurd; the concept requires the world's refusal. Longing alone is just appetite — tragedy needs the locked door.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Appetite without obstacle is merely hunger, fed or feedable. The absurd is the locked door experienced by the hungry — remove the lock and only appetite remains.
items.lessonContent:
Appetites need obstacles to become tragic.
Locked doors complete hunger's drama.
Satisfaction dissolves what refusal creates.
Single terms never make relations.
Share this: find one hunger with no lock.

items.title: The Worst Labor
items.question: Camus opens by calling Sisyphus's fate horrible: the gods designed futile, hopeless labor as the ultimate punishment.
items.correctExplanation: True. The opening grants the horror fully — futile endless toil as the gods' worst invention. Only then does revolt invert it; the happiness lands because the horror was conceded.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Camus never minimizes: 'the horrible punishment' stands unsoftened. Concession precedes inversion — happiness means something only against admitted horror.
items.lessonContent:
Concede horror before inverting it.
Unsoftened premises make real conclusions.
Inversion needs weight to work against.
Never minimize what you mean to transcend.
Share this: admit one horror fully today.

items.title: The Lucid Wound
items.question: Sisyphus's consciousness of his fate is simultaneously his tragedy and his victory — it makes the torment real and makes revolt possible.
items.correctExplanation: True. Unconscious rolling would be mere mechanics; lucid rolling is tragedy owned — and ownership is victory. Consciousness wounds and crowns at once.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The rock crushes, but awareness converts crushing into confrontation: tragedy admitted becomes triumph chosen. One faculty, two edges — the wound that is also the crown.
items.lessonContent:
Awareness wounds and crowns together.
Owned tragedy converts to chosen triumph.
Mechanics become meaning through lucidity.
Single faculties cut both ways.
Share this: own one torment consciously.

items.title: The Just Gods
items.question: Oedipus concludes that the gods treated him justly, and Camus endorses this theodicy as the myth's true moral.
items.correctExplanation: False. Oedipus concludes 'all is well' — fate become his own matter — not that gods were fair. Camus endorses lucid ownership, never divine justice.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The essay's Oedipus finds everything his own, not everything just: 'all is well' means fate internalized, not gods vindicated. Theodicy is another consolation revolt refuses.
items.lessonContent:
Ownership differs from vindication entirely.
'All is well' internalizes; it never absolves.
Theodicy is consolation in disguise.
Read conclusions for what they actually claim.
Share this: own one fate without justifying it.

items.title: The Unconsoled
items.question: Camusian revolt permanently refuses consolation — no hope, no faith, no future settlement may soften the lucid confrontation.
items.correctExplanation: True. Consolation dissolves tension, and tension is the required state. The unconsoled stance holds through every offered comfort.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Hopes, faiths, and settlements all exit through the same door: they end the confrontation revolt must maintain. Refusal is permanent because the condition is.
items.lessonContent:
Comforts that end tension are exits.
Permanence matches the permanent condition.
Refusal maintained is revolt defined.
Softening is surrender spelled kindly.
Share this: refuse one softening today.

items.title: The Empty Detachment
items.question: Meursault's emotional detachment proves that, for Camus, nothing matters at all — not sun, sea, friendship, or sensory joy.
items.correctExplanation: False. Meursault loves swimming, sunlight, Marie — his honesty is about feeling truly, not feeling nothing. Detachment from lies, attachment to senses.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The Stranger's crime is refusing comforting falsehoods, not lacking love: sun, sea, and Marie fill him genuinely. Honesty about feeling differs totally from absence of it.
items.lessonContent:
Honesty about feeling differs from feeling nothing.
Refusing lies is not refusing life.
Senses fill whom sermons leave empty.
Read detachment for its actual object.
Share this: love one sunlight honestly.

items.title: The Limitless Emperor
items.question: Caligula's murders and defiance show that absurd freedom recognizes no limits whatsoever — the logical endpoint Camus celebrates.
items.correctExplanation: False. Caligula is the cautionary inversion: freedom pushed past revolt's limits destroys what revolt protects. Camus stages the endpoint to condemn it.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. The play exhibits absurd logic weaponized — and self-devouring. Endpoints that eat their own foundations warn; revolt's limits (no murder) are the lesson Caligula's corpse teaches.
items.lessonContent:
Endpoints that devour foundations warn, not beckon.
Weaponized logic self-destructs on schedule.
Limits protect revolt from its own emperors.
Stage extremes to condemn them.
Share this: spot one freedom eating itself.
